Paleomagnetism and rock magnetism of ~2.37–1.89 Ga dykes from the
Western Dharwar craton, southern India: Implications for drift history
through paleoproterozic
Venkateshwarlu Mamillaa,b,*, Ramesh Babu Nathia
aCSIR-National Geophysical Research Institute, Uppal Road, Hyderabad 500007, India
bAcademy of Scientific and Innovative Research (AcSIR), Ghaziabad 201002, India
A R T I C L E I N F O A B S T R A C T
Keywords: Astudy has been carried out using Paleomagnetism and rock magnetism as a proxy on dykes from Tiptur area in
Rock Magnetism the late Archean Western Dharwar craton, southern India.101 oriented block samples from 20 sites (10 sites (cid:0)
Paleomagnetism 50 samples from Belagumba and 10 sites (cid:0) 51 samples from Navile) of NE-SW and NNW-SSE oriented dykes were
Dharwar craton
collected and the results are presented here along with previously reported data on dyke swarms from Western as
Paleoproterozoic
well as Eastern Dharwar craton. Measurement of magnetisation versus temperature curves yielded two types of
thermo-magnetic curves which are nearly reversible and irreversible with magnetite as remanence carrierfor
both Belagumba and Navile dykes. The magnetic directions show two components, viz., six sites representing
Belagumba dyke give mean declination of 269◦ and mean inclination of (cid:0) 38◦ (Precision parameter (k) =9,
Circle of confidence (α 95) =23◦) and nine sites from Navile dyke yielded mean declination of 302◦and mean
inclination of (cid:0) 21◦(k =44, α 95 =8◦). The corresponding paleopoles obtained at 6.09◦S, 325◦E (semi-axis of the
ellipse of confidence (dp) =16◦and semi-axis perpendicular to the great circle (dm) =27◦) for Belagumba and
27◦N, 327◦E (dp =4◦and dm =8◦) for Navile respectively. The updated APWP for Dharwar craton from two
polesfrom this study and six well constrained key paleopoles from 2.37 Ga to 1.89 Ga periodsof previous studies
suggests that Dharwar craton has a rapid drift rate from 26◦to 53◦paleolatitude along with a clockwise rotation
(~40◦) during 2235 Ma to 2216 Ma.
1. Introduction that records Earth’s history dating back to about 3.4 billion years. The
southern part of the peninsular India is occupied by high-grade granulite
Dyke swarms serve as a major geologic feature to represent as crustal terrain and a major craton to its north is called the Dharwar craton. The
extensions which have been formed by virtue of pouring out of large Dharwar craton is mainly composed of Archean gneisses and low-grade
volumes of mantle material. Mafic dyke swarms represent short lived greenstone belts. Based on the lithological and tectonic differences
magmatic events through which the mantle materials are emplaced into Dharwar craton is divided into Eastern Dharwar craton (EDC) and
the crust. The formation of mafic dykes is usually related to Large Western Dharwar craton (WDC) by the 2500 Ma closepet granite (Gupta
Igneous Provinces (LIP) or a passive rifting event or a mantle plume et al., 2003a). The Dharwar craton is cut across by numerous mafic dyke
activity. Mafic dykes are necessarily connected to deep Earth dynamics swarms like in other Archean cratons worldwide. These dykes represent
and supercontinent cyclicity (Ernst et al., 2001; Ernst, 2014; Buchan and crustal extension episodes during which basaltic material derived from
Ernst, 2018). Mafic dykes are extensively intruded into Earth’s conti- the mantle is transferred to the continental crust. The study of these
nental crust and occurs as major swarms, especially in the Precambrian dykes will help to understand the nature and composition of the mantle
terranes like the Canadian shield, West Australian Yilgarn craton, the source. Of the six Archean to early Proterozoic cratons in the Indian
Archean complexes of East Antarctica and India (Bateman et al., 2001; shield, the Dharwar craton in the south is most extensive and well pre-
French and Heaman, 2010; Mikhalsky et al., 2013). served. The Dharwar craton is one of the oldest and widely studied
Southern peninsular India forms one of the oldest continental crust Archean cratons of the Peninsular India and it is a classic granite-
